doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Gigs at other colleges and the burning car at Union
summary: The early Catatonic Five mostly played on campus; at Union they burned a car to give Dave Barbour light to read music, and Derry Hall wrote arrangements.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Right. Well Phil described some of the going out on weekends and playing on other campuses. I assume you guys did the same thing?

Yes but not to the same extent that the second incarnation of the Catatonic Five. My early incarnation of the Catatonic Five played mostly on the campus. We occasionally played at other colleges. We played at Union on one occasion and this is an example of how the alcohol situation got out of control. Dave Barbour was the pianist and he needed to read music. And our alcoholic consumption had got to a stage where it seemed to be a good idea, since we were playing out on the front lawn of this fraternity house, to set fire to a car that we have illumination and Barbour could read the music. It was an old car but it © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
was the wrong thing to do, and we had to flee and the police came after us but they never caught us. But anyway.
Much better than stand lights I guess.
It was a flickering — it was a stupid thing.
Uh huh. It must have been hard, because your piano player had to have sheet music, it must have really put a limiting factor on what songs you could play obviously, because he had to have the sheet.

It did. But perhaps he had taken our songs and somebody had scored it. Derry Hall could write music like nobody else and so he could do that. We used to play weirdoes like the “Indian Love Call” and stuff like that. And it would be written out and Barbour would play it. We were not a very good band. We were just an early band.

The second one, the Fallacious Five was first, we were the second, and then we all graduated or went in the Army and then the Donn Andre-Phil Mead band, the second incarnation, which was a really good band, brought a claim to Hamilton. They really went around internationally under the banner of Hamilton so it was good for the college.
